content: The results of HPV nucleic acid testing (HPV DNA or mRNA tests) will soon be integrated into updated guidelines. These guidelines will combine recommendations from two 2021 publications on the use of HPV DNA and mRNA tests, along with forthcoming recommendations on screening and treatment strategies (Phase 3). This will culminate in a comprehensive living guideline (Phase 4). In 2006, the World Health Organization (WHO) released the Comprehensive Cervical Cancer Control: A Guide to Essential Practice (C4GEP), which was updated in 2014. This document consolidated recommendations for cervical cancer prevention and treatment, including HPV vaccination, management of cervical cancer and precancerous lesions, and palliative care. It also incorporated earlier guidelines from 2013 on screening and treating precancerous cervical lesions. In 2019, WHO issued guidance on using thermal ablation for treating cervical precancerous lesions. In 2020, additional documents were published to support the implementation and scaling up of screening and treatment interventions, particularly those involving HPV testing and related medical devices. The updated guidelines distinguish between two populations: women living with HIV and the general population of women (those presumed or confirmed to be HIV-negative or with unknown HIV status). Two approaches to screening and treatment are outlined: the screen-and-treat approach, where treatment is based solely on a positive primary screening test, and the screen, triage, and treat approach, where treatment decisions are based on a positive primary test followed by a positive triage test, with or without histological confirmation. For women eligible for ablative treatment, it is recommended to perform the procedure during the same visit as the screening test (single-visit approach). However, in facilities where this is not feasible, a second visit may be required (two-visit approach). If excisional treatment, such as LLETZ (Large Loop Excision of the Transformation Zone), is unavailable on-site, women should be referred for further evaluation or treatment. In the screen, triage, and treat approach, a triage test is conducted after a positive primary screening test. Treatment is recommended only if both tests are positive. A positive triage test may lead to colposcopy with biopsy and histopathological examination to determine the appropriate treatment. However, the implementation of colposcopy and biopsy can be challenging, so alternative triage strategies that do not rely on colposcopy are also considered. If the triage test is negative, women should undergo follow-up evaluation at specified intervals. The term LLETZ is used in this guideline to refer to the excision of the transformation zone. In some countries, the term LEEP (Loop Electrosurgical Excision Procedure) is used interchangeably. For cervical cancer prevention in the general population, WHO suggests using HPV DNA detection in a screen-and-treat approach starting at age 30, with regular screening every 5 to 10 years. For women living with HIV, WHO recommends HPV DNA detection in a screen, triage, and treat approach starting at age 25, with regular screening every 3 to 5 years. No recommendation was made for using HPV mRNA testing in women living with HIV. For triage after a positive HPV DNA test in women living with HIV, WHO suggests using partial genotyping, colposcopy, VIA (visual inspection with acetic acid), or cytology. The updated guidelines were developed following WHO's rigorous methodology, as outlined in the WHO Handbook for Guideline Development. The process involved contributions from various expert groups, including the Guideline Development Group (GDG), External Review Group (ERG), systematic review teams, and modeling teams. The GDG included 53 members with diverse expertise in cervical screening and treatment, representing all six WHO regions and including civil society representatives and women living with HIV. The recommendations were formulated based on evidence synthesized from systematic reviews, mathematical modeling, and stakeholder input. The GDG reached consensus on all recommendations, which were categorized as either strong (WHO recommends) or conditional (WHO suggests) based on the balance of benefits and harms. The guideline emphasizes the importance of evidence-based strategies for cervical cancer prevention and recognizes the need for inclusive language. While most evidence is based on studies involving cisgender women, the term women is used to refer to all individuals at risk for cervical cancer, including transgender men, non-binary individuals, and others with a female reproductive system. The target audience for this document includes policymakers, program managers, healthcare professionals, and community health workers involved in cervical cancer prevention. It may also serve as a resource for developing materials to support women and their families in making informed decisions about screening and treatment. The guideline underscores the right to equality and non-discrimination in sexual and reproductive healthcare.
